markets.role: São Paulo is Latin America's biggest art room and its most liquid. The Art Basel/UBS 2026 report found Brazilian galleries' sales up 21% in 2025, and 23% of Brazilian collectors started within the past five years, the highest share in the 2025 survey. The rooms are SP-Arte (22nd edition, April 2026, more than 180 exhibitors in Niemeyer's Biennial pavilion, with design grown from 23 to 64 stands since 2016), its August sibling SP-Arte Rotas, and a gallery tier — Luisa Strina, Nara Roesler, Fortes D'Aloia & Gabriel, Mendes Wood DM, Vermelho — that sells more abroad than any other in the region; US customs recorded US$154m of art arriving from Brazil in 2025, US$124m of it paintings. Buyers are domestic: the fair's founder calls it ‘a market accustomed to crises’, and the international galleries present are few. What bites: Brazil's import duties and state taxes on foreign art (a well-known deterrent, not sourced here), the real, and a presidential election in October 2026 that made collectors cautious at ArtRio.
src: Trading Economics (UN Comtrade), US imports from Brazil, 2025

markets.role: Rio is the second Brazilian room, smaller and more local than São Paulo. ArtRio's 16th edition at Marina da Glória (September 2026) had 76 galleries, largely Brazilian, with sales reported from a pre-preview dinner and no totals disclosed; artistic director Maria Luz Bridger said the market was ‘doing really well’ even as some collectors held back before the October 2026 presidential vote. The galleries that define the city are artist-founded A Gentil Carioca (Márcio Botner), Anita Schwartz's gallery of nearly 30 years, and the Rio spaces of São Paulo houses such as Nara Roesler and Fortes D'Aloia & Gabriel (the latter from memory). Brazil is Latin America's second-largest art market by the Art Basel/UBS count, and the collector base is young: 23% began within five years. What bites is the same as in São Paulo — import taxes on foreign work, the currency and the electoral cycle — plus Rio's dependence on a single fair week for international visitors.

Mexico City is the region's most international market and the one most exposed to the United States. Zona Maco, in its 24th year at Centro Banamex in February 2026, drew more than 75 museum groups, many from the US and Canada, and a gallery news page put the exhibitor count at 241 (headline); the same week carries Material and Salón Acme. Prices run from Kouri + Corrao's $500 to Sean Kelly's $300,000 for Abramović and Wiley, with Pace selling almost a whole Kylie Manning solo stand at the preview, one triptych to a Mexican collection. Dealers describe a split: fewer US collectors than in past years (Kates-Ferri) but Americans attending ‘partly to escape the political climate at home’ (Sean Kelly), and a steady rise in international visitors over six to eight years (Galería de Arte Mexicano). The local tier — kurimanzutto, OMR, Labor, Proyectos Monclova — and the house Morton Subastas were not covered in the pages opened. What bites: dependence on dollar buyers, the peso, and US tariff policy, even though art itself is exempt from the 2026 tariff regime; Mexico's declared HS 9701 exports were only US$2.4m in 2025, so most Mexican art sold abroad leaves through the galleries' foreign spaces.

Buenos Aires is a peso market with a deep collecting tradition and little international money. arteBA 2025 (28–31 August, Centro Costa Salguero) had 67 galleries, more than 400 artists and 11,000 m², with an International Dialogue Zone of galleries from São Paulo, Paris and Miami, and museum and corporate acquisition programmes published before the opening; the Premio VOLF paid ARS 3,000,000. The anchor is Ruth Benzacar, 60 years old in 2025 and run by Orly Benzacar and Mora Bacal, alongside a younger tier such as Moria; the auction side (Roldán Moderno) was not covered in the pages opened. Buyers are Argentine families, corporations and museums buying through the fair's acquisition schemes. What bites: inflation and the gap between official and parallel dollar rates (from memory, not sourced here), export paperwork for cultural goods, and the thinness of foreign demand — Argentina declared only US$1.2m of HS 9701 exports in 2025.

Bogotá is a market that peaked a decade ago and has shrunk to a curated core. ARTBO, run by the Bogotá Chamber of Commerce, held its 21st edition on 24–28 September 2025 at Agora Bogotá with 46 galleries, about half the count at the peak, under a new director, Jaime A. Martínez, who succeeded María Paz Gaviria after ten years; the inaugural Bogotá Biennial ran alongside. Reported prices were modest — Mor Charpentier $15,000–60,000 for Porter, López and Maravilla; 193 Gallery $5,500–16,500; Vermelho $4,000–18,000; Galería Extra $3,000–10,000 — and a monumental textile by María Sosa was reserved within an hour. Casas Riegner's Paula Bossa: ‘Colombia's art market is complicated.’ What bites: the 2023 peso devaluation, inflation, politics, a cautious domestic base with few collectors and limited budgets, and shipping and customs that once forced galleries to route through Miami (now easier, says Vermelho's Eduardo Brandão). Colombia declared US$0.95m of HS 9701 exports in 2025.

Lima is the smallest of the seven Latin American rooms here and the least documented in the pages opened. Its galleries are visible abroad rather than at home: Crisis Galería's director Juan Luis Balarezo showed at SP-Arte 2026 and argued that ‘there shouldn't be a premium on so-called Western art’, and Livia Benavides Gallery sold into Zona Maco 2026. Art Lima, the fair founded in 2013 (memory), could not be confirmed as having held a 2025 or 2026 edition. Peru declared US$1.9m of HS 9701 exports in 2025, more than Colombia or Argentina, consistent with a handful of galleries exporting through fairs. Buyers are a small group of Lima collectors and the museums MALI and MAC (memory). What bites: political instability, the absence of a reliable fair week, and the cost of shipping to the regional fairs that provide most sales. Treat this paragraph as a sketch: only the two gallery quotes and the trade figure are sourced.

Santiago's market runs through one fair. Ch.ACO held its 15th edition in March 2025 with more than 200 artists and its 16th in March 2026 in Vitacura with more than 250 artists from 16 countries and galleries from 11 countries, billed as the largest in its history; The Art Newspaper describes the fair as foregrounding affordable work, often with a political edge, and as aiming to be a focal point for South American art (all headlines; pages not opened). The galleries — Patricia Ready, Die Ecke and others — are from memory, as is the absence of any auction house of note. Buyers are Chilean collectors and a growing museum presence at the fair (headline). Chile declared US$3.4m of HS 9701 exports in 2025, above Argentina and Colombia. What bites: a small collector base, the peso, and distance from the regional circuit, which Ch.ACO tries to answer by positioning itself as the southern cone's international meeting point.

Lagos is West Africa's market and its most volatile. ART X Lagos reached its 10th edition on 6–9 November 2025 at the Federal Palace Hotel with 15 exhibitors — 11 from Lagos and four from Uganda, Cameroon, Ghana and the UK — down from nearly twice as many in earlier editions after the selection was streamlined from 2023; the fair draws 10,000–12,000 visitors a year and released an impact report in October 2025. Founder Tokini Peterside-Schwebig said the city needed ‘a major catalyst’; she was optimistic about sales because the naira had strengthened. The galleries that travel are Kó (prices from $2,000 to $7,500 at Cape Town in February 2026), O'Da Art (from $4,000), Rele and SMO (the last two from memory); Arthouse Contemporary is the auction room (memory). Buyers are Nigeria's business elite (African Business headline) and the diaspora, with London — 1-54 and Bonhams' African sales — as the price-setting room. What bites: the naira crisis and inflation, a soft global market in which ‘works from Africa are particularly affected’, and the absence of Nigeria from the world's top-100 HS 9701 exporters, meaning most Nigerian art is exported through London and Accra rather than declared at Lagos.

Cape Town is Africa's largest fair city and the continent's secondary-market capital shared with Johannesburg. The Investec Cape Town Art Fair's 13th edition (20–22 February 2026, CTICC) had 126 galleries from 34 cities, 42 of them debuting, more than 490 artists and about 34,000 visitors, with works from EUR 600 to close to EUR 250,000 — Southern Guild's Zanele Muholi editions from $25,000, WHATIFTHEWORLD's Dan Halter at EUR 5,000–20,000, 99 Loop's Barry Yusufu at EUR 4,000–16,000. Director Laura Vincenti says ‘the somewhat fashionable wave of so-called African art is gradually subsiding’ while local collecting matures. Strauss & Co's Cape Town saleroom sold Irma Stern's ‘Malay (Black Headdress)’ for R21.7m (US$1.26m) in October 2025, part of a record R475.5m (US$28m) year, up 26%, on 6,927 lots. Buyers are South African, with growing European and American interest and Business Day calling the domestic secondary market ‘a picture of health’ (13 Feb 2026 headline). What bites: the rand, export permits for older works, and South Africa's modest declared trade — US$14.6m of HS 9701 exports in 2025.

Johannesburg is where Africa's highest auction prices are made. Strauss & Co's flagship sales are held here: Vladimir Tretchikoff's ‘Lady from the Orient’ (1955) made R31.1m (US$1.8m) in May 2025 after 89 bids, a world record for the artist, and the November auction week closes the house's year; digital auctions now carry most of its 6,927 lots, and the house opened Kenya with an inaugural auction in 2025. The gallery tier — Goodman (with London and New York), Stevenson (with Cape Town and Amsterdam), Everard Read, Afronova (Dimakatso Mathopa from EUR 4,800 at Cape Town 2026) — and the second house, Aspire Art, are largely from memory, as is FNB Art Joburg, the September fair whose 2025 figures were not found. Buyers are corporate collections, Johannesburg families and increasingly foreign bidders drawn by Strauss's European marketing. What bites: the rand, crime and infrastructure (memory), and a domestic economy whose ‘improving outlook’ Strauss credits for restoring consignor confidence in 2025.

Accra is a one-gallery hub. Gallery 1957 is the node: listed as a 2025 exhibitor at ART X Lagos, present in Art Basel's gallery catalogue and on Artsy, reported by Artforum to have opened a second Accra space and by Art Daily to be extending its influence as far as Hong Kong (all headlines or listings; no page opened). Around it sit the Nubuke Foundation and ADA \ contemporary (memory). Ghana declared US$7.1m of HS 9701 exports in 2025 — more than South Africa's neighbours and close to Thailand — a sign that Accra's painters (Amoako Boafo's generation, memory) leave through the gallery to London and the fairs. Buyers are overwhelmingly foreign; the domestic collector base is thin. What bites: a market built on a few names whose prices rose fast in 2020–22 and have since cooled with the wider African segment, the cedi, and the dependence on London (1-54, Bonhams) and Cape Town for sales rooms. Treat as a sketch.
src: ART X Lagos exhibitor listing (not opened)

markets.role: Nairobi's market is an auction-and-gallery hybrid at small scale. Circle Art Gallery runs the Modern and Contemporary East African Art Auction (a 2026 edition is tagged by Start Journal on 18 March 2026; page not opened), and Strauss & Co of Cape Town held its inaugural auction in Kenya in 2025, the first entry of a continental house into East Africa. Kenya's declared art trade shows where the money goes: in 2023 the country exported US$6.45m of HS 97, 66% of it (US$4.27m) to the United Kingdom and 25% (US$1.65m) to the United States, and imported just US$0.83m, nearly half from China. The galleries — Circle, One Off, the Nairobi Contemporary Art Institute — are from memory beyond Circle's auction. Buyers are expatriates, the Kenyan professional class and London-based collectors of East African modernism. What bites: the shilling, a tiny domestic base, and the fact that Kenya's HS 9701 exports were only US$0.4m in 2025, so most value leaves as consignments to London rather than as declared sales.

Marrakech is the African fair city with the most institutional scaffolding. 1-54 Marrakech's 7th edition (5–8 February 2026, La Mamounia) had 22 galleries from 12 countries and more than 60 artists from 21, with Moroccan artists over half the programme and seven Morocco-based galleries (Loft Art Gallery and L'Atelier 21 of Casablanca among them); DaDa ran a parallel show to 30 March, and MACAAL, LE 18, the Musée Yves Saint Laurent and Fondation TGCC's Prix Mustaqbal (five editions, 70+ artists) exhibited the same week. Christie's lists the fair among its partner events. The domestic trade is Casablanca's: the galleries and the auction house CMOOA (memory) price Moroccan modernism for Moroccan buyers, while 1-54 brings European collectors to the riads. Morocco declared US$3.8m of HS 9701 exports in 2025 and US$2.6m of HS 97 exports to the United States, mostly collectors' pieces. What bites: foreign-exchange controls on dirham accounts (memory), customs on imported works, and a visitor-driven fair whose sales depend on the February tourist week.
src: Trading Economics (UN Comtrade), Morocco exports to US, 2025

markets.role: Cairo has a showcase but not yet a market. Art D'Égypte's ‘Forever Is Now’ held its fifth edition at the Giza Pyramids in October–November 2025 with ten artists and has announced a return in 2026 (headlines), and the Cairo International Art District is expanding downtown (Egyptian Streets, 28 Oct 2025 headline); none of this is a sales fair. The trade sits in Zamalek — Safarkhan for Egyptian modern painting, Gypsum for contemporary (both from memory) — and in the Egyptian modern sales at Christie's and Sotheby's in London and Dubai (memory). Egypt declared only US$0.4m of HS 9701 exports in 2025, the lowest of the African cities here. Buyers are Gulf and Egyptian-diaspora collectors for the moderns (Mahmoud Saïd's generation) and a small Cairo base for the living. What bites: hard-currency scarcity and import restrictions since the 2023 pound devaluation (memory), export rules on anything deemed heritage, and the lack of a fair, which leaves Art D'Égypte's pyramid show as the only international week. Treat as a sketch.

London is where African art is priced. 1-54 held its 2025 London edition on 16–19 October at Somerset House with 100 artists (headline) and has a 2026 edition listed; October Gallery and Vigo are regulars, and the fair's Marrakech and New York editions extend the brand. Bonhams' Modern & Contemporary African Art department under Helene Love-Allotey held its autumn live sale on 8 October 2025 at New Bond Street, estimating Ben Enwonwu's ‘Negritude’ and a 1994 Kentridge drawing at £150,000–200,000 each and Clara Etso Ugbodaga-Ngu at £100,000–150,000, timed to Tate Modern's Nigerian Modernism opening the same day; results were not read. The customs data confirm the hub: Kenya sends 66% of its declared art exports to the UK, and Nigeria and Ghana's painters reach buyers through London galleries rather than declared exports. What bites: the UK's 5% import VAT on art (memory), post-2020 customs on EU consignments, and a soft segment in which ‘works from Africa are particularly affected’ (The Art Newspaper, Nov 2025).

Taipei is a rich collector city that has just lost its international fair. Taipei Dangdai, launched in 2019 (memory) and owned by The Art Assembly (memory), announced in autumn 2025 that it would not return in 2026; Art Taipei, run by the Taiwan Art Gallery Association, held its 2025 edition on 23–27 October at the World Trade Centre, where Hong Kong dealer Pascal de Sarthe judged that it ‘delivered’ with ‘satisfying’ sales, and a 2026 edition with a Japanese section is announced. The money is real: a Taiwanese collector is believed to have paid HK$197m (US$25.4m) for a Picasso in Hong Kong in September 2025, the stock market is booming and the New Taiwan dollar is strong. The domestic houses — Ravenel, Zhong Cheng, Kingsley — sell Taiwanese and Chinese modern art to local families (from memory; no 2025 totals opened). Taiwan declared only US$4.9m of HS 9701 exports in 2025: Taiwanese buyers import through Hong Kong and consign there. What bites: a three-year global downturn that killed the fair, cross-strait risk, and the island's dependence on Hong Kong salerooms for anything above the domestic ceiling.

Jakarta is Southeast Asia's largest domestic market and its most inward-looking. Art Jakarta 2026 (2–4 October, JIExpo Kemayoran, three halls) had 75 galleries — 42 Indonesian and 33 international, 19 of them new — and added AJScope, six independent initiatives backed by the Culture Ministry, and AJX institutional collaborations; the 2025 edition drew an ‘impressive turnout’ despite a weak market and social unrest (SCMP headline). Visitor and sales totals were not published in the pages opened. The rooms beyond the fair are the auction house Larasati (Jakarta and Singapore), galleries such as ROH Projects, and the private Museum MACAN (all memory). Buyers are Indonesian-Chinese collecting families who buy Indonesian modern and contemporary at home and Western names in Hong Kong and Singapore (memory); Singapore's 2023 customs show the corridor, with Jakarta money moving through the Freeport and the Singapore houses. Indonesia does not appear among the world's top-100 HS 9701 exporters. What bites: import duty and luxury tax on foreign art (memory), the rupiah, and a market whose international galleries come for Indonesian buyers rather than to sell Indonesians abroad.
src: South China Morning Post, Oct 2025 (headline only)

markets.role: Bangkok is building institutions faster than a market. The Bangkok Art Biennale held its fourth edition in 2024 across temples and museums (headlines), Bangkok Kunsthalle and Khao Yai Art Forest opened as ‘two new art institutions in Thailand’ (Culture360 headline) with the collector Marisa Chearavanont profiled by Numéro (20 Jun 2025) as the figure behind Khao Yai, and Artnet asked whether Bangkok could be ‘the next Miami’ (headline). The commercial tier — Nova Contemporary, Bangkok CityCity, and the newer dealer spaces — and the absence of an auction house are from memory; ArtReview's ‘true state of Bangkok's art ecosystem’ was not opened. Thailand declared US$7.4m of HS 9701 exports in 2025, more than Taiwan, Vietnam or the Philippines. Buyers are Thai-Chinese families and the hospitality groups commissioning for hotels; international galleries arrive through the Biennale rather than a fair. What bites: the lack of a fair of scale, import VAT and duty on foreign works (memory), the baht, and a market that so far monetises art through tourism and patronage rather than sales.

Manila is a fair-and-auction market built on local masters. Art Fair Philippines moved into Circuit Corporate Center One in Circuit Makati for its February 2026 edition (6–8 February; the 13th by Vogue's count, two years after The Art Newspaper called 2025 the ‘11th edition in new venue’) with around 55 galleries from the Philippines and abroad; recent editions drew 25,000–30,000 visitors, nearly a third students, and the district is to gain a Contemporary Art Center. Returning exhibitors were León Gallery, Galerie Stephanie, J Studio, White Walls and Orange Project; National Artists BenCab, Jose Joya and Ang Kiukok were on the walls. The auction side — León Gallery and Salcedo Auctions, which set the records for Philippine modernists (memory) — was not covered in the pages opened; Silverlens is the gallery with a New York space (memory). The Philippines declared US$4.6m of HS 9701 exports in 2025, and Hong Kong customs record Philippine art arriving (page listed, not opened). What bites: a market priced in pesos for a domestic elite, import duties on foreign art (memory) and the small number of international galleries willing to travel.
src: Trading Economics (UN Comtrade), Hong Kong imports from Philippines (not opened)

markets.role: Vietnam's market is priced abroad. The Indochina School painters — Lê Phổ, Mai Trung Thu, Vũ Cao Đàm, Nguyen Gia Tri — sell at Sotheby's and Christie's in Hong Kong and at Aguttes in Paris: Mai Trung Thu's ‘Portrait of Mademoiselle Phuong’ made a record US$3.1m (VietnamPlus, 2021), a Lê Phổ US$2.369m (Hanoi Times) and Nguyen Gia Tri ‘breaks international auction records’ (Hanoi Times), while a Sotheby's Hong Kong Southeast Asian spring series totalled HK$85m (US$11m) (press-release headline; year not stated). At home the rooms are galleries — Galerie Quynh in Ho Chi Minh City since 2003, Manzi in Hanoi (memory) — and no auction house of scale; Vietnam declared US$7.2m of HS 9701 exports in 2025. Buyers are Vietnamese new money repatriating the moderns and the diaspora in Paris and California (memory). What bites: authenticity disputes around the Indochina School (memory), export permits for older works, state limits on foreign exchange, and the absence of a fair, so Hanoi and Saigon remain supply towns for Hong Kong and Paris.

Pakistan's market is split between home galleries and foreign salerooms. The 2025 South Asian season set the frame: Saffronart's $40.2m sale in New Delhi (27 September) and Sotheby's $25.5m sale (29 September) were records, M.F. Husain's $13.7m at Christie's in March the highest for an Indian painting, and dealers count 15–20 clients worldwide buying South Asian works above $1m; within that, Sadequain and Chughtai are named as artists who ‘break out of regional collecting’ and Anwar Jalal Shemza as attracting Indian buyers (no Pakistani prices given). At Art Dubai, Arab News reports, Pakistani artists ‘find the space missing at home’ (2025 headline). Karachi's Canvas Gallery and Sanat Initiative and Lahore's galleries are from memory, as is the absence of a domestic auction house; Grosvenor Gallery in London (Charles Moore) is the specialist dealer. Pakistan is not among the top-100 HS 9701 exporters. What bites: rupee weakness and foreign-exchange controls, customs on imported works, the political stand-off that keeps Indian buyers and Pakistani sellers in third-country rooms (Dubai, London), and India's September 2025 GST cut to 5% that favours Delhi and Mumbai as the subcontinent's salerooms.

Dhaka is a city of 36.6 million with few commercial galleries and, from November 2026, a first art fair. Art Dhaka (6–10 November 2026, at Aloki, a cultural hub in a former garment factory) was founded by the collector Durjoy Rahman with Nahar Khan, Aumia Khundkar and Aloki's founder Fahd Sattar, curated by Najmun Nahar Keya and Zihan Khan, to reach ‘new and younger Bangladeshi collectors’. It steps into the gap left by the Dhaka Art Summit, the Samdani Art Foundation's non-commercial platform held since 2012 and last staged in 2023, with no date for a return. The galleries are Drik, Galleri Kaya, Gallery Chitrak and Abinta. Prices are made in London: two of the highest prices ever paid for Bangladeshi works, both Zainul Abedin pieces of 1970, sold at Sotheby's London in September 2025 (amounts not stated), and The Art Newspaper reported in April 2025 that ‘long undervalued Bangladeshi artists begin to rise at auction’ (headline). What bites: politics — Sheikh Hasina's ouster in 2024, an interim government, and a February 2026 election won by the BNP — economic strain, and a currency and customs regime that keeps foreign galleries away.
